name: GHC Haskell lightweight threads (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (GHC thread versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per thread (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 900x-1,460x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Haskell side: stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (github.com/ghc/ghc is a read-only mirror of gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc, which was not opened)
tradeoffs: GHC threads are heap-allocated stack chunks scheduled by the GHC runtime (garbage-collected, optional -threaded and -N). Foreign calls and unsafe FFI interact with the scheduler differently from C.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. The repo_url is the GHC compiler mirror because the claim is about the compiler/runtime; the skynet Haskell source is haskell/ in atemerev/skynet. The license file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Haskell row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: GHC threads are runtime-scheduled green threads, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

name: NPB-Rust (NAS Parallel Benchmarks in Rust, sequential and Rayon)
baseline: NPB-CPP, the group's C++ port of NAS Parallel Benchmarks 3.4.1 (sequential NPB-SER, and OpenMP NPB-OMP for the parallel comparison), plus the original Fortran NPB
workload: NAS Parallel Benchmarks kernels EP, CG, MG, IS, FT and pseudo-applications BT, SP, LU in Rust (sequential NPB-RUST and Rayon-parallel NPB-RAYON), compared with the C++ and Fortran versions.
claimed_speedup: From the paper abstract as shown in a search snippet (snippet only): Rust sequential is 5.59% faster than C++ and 1.23% slower than Fortran; Rust with Rayon is slower than both the Fortran and the C++ OpenMP versions.
compiler_and_flags: Rust: toolchain 1.85.0 or newer, cargo build --release (repo README); C++ and Fortran compilers and flags unknown
tradeoffs: Rust port of NPB with a sequential variant (NPB-RUST) and a Rayon variant (NPB-RAYON); safety and ergonomics trade-offs are not discussed on the pages that were opened.
caveats: The arXiv page (2502.15536) is blocked in this environment and was not opened; the numbers come from a WebSearch snippet of arxiv.org/html/2502.15536v1 (snippet only), so the venue, peer-review status, hardware and flags are unconfirmed and a verifier with paper access should retier. The GitHub repo page has no performance numbers. The only win over C++ is the sequential aggregate (5.59%, a small margin); the concurrency part (Rayon versus C++ OpenMP) is a loss, so the category fit is weak and the entry belongs more to numerics/safety if kept. The C++ baseline is the same group's NPB-CPP port (FGCS 2021, https://github.com/GMAP/NPB-CPP, whose README says it matches original NPB performance).
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust Rayon vs C++ OpenMP TBB performance comparison paper NAS Parallel Benchmarks Rust faster' surfaced arXiv 2502.15536; opened the GMAP/NPB-Rust and GMAP/NPB-CPP repos.

name: Tokio (1M concurrent tasks, peak memory)
baseline: Asio C++20 coroutines (awaitable tasks) and concurrencpp
workload: Spawn N concurrent async tasks that wait on a timer and measure peak memory (port of the Rust '1 million concurrent tasks' memory benchmark to C++ coroutine libraries).
claimed_speedup: Peak memory at 1M tasks: tokio 214,136 KB, concurrencpp 605,972 KB, Asio 853,144 KB (about 2.8x and 4.0x less, derived from page data); at 100k tasks: 23,824 vs 61,460 vs 86,652 KB; at 10k: 6,908 vs 7,840 vs 10,244 KB. At 1 task tokio is the largest (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB). Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M.
compiler_and_flags: C++20 with coroutines, compiler not named, CMake Release default, no flags listed; Rust build via cargo (profile unstated)
hardware: Intel i7-8550U (8 threads, about 1.99 GHz), 8 GB RAM, WSL Ubuntu 20.04.6 on Windows 10
tradeoffs: Tokio tasks are stackless futures sized by the compiler, so memory is small per task but not free of heap allocation per spawn; the C++ libraries allocate a coroutine frame per task. The result is about memory only, not throughput or latency.
caveats: Independent hobby replication (4 stars, 6 commits, last commit 2023-06-24), not the tokio authors' benchmark. The README says the original article's methodology was criticised and the author replicated it anyway. Compiler, Asio and concurrencpp versions and flags are unstated; WSL on a laptop CPU, run count not stated. Tokio loses at 1 task. The tokio repo page (opened) makes no comparison to C++ runtimes. Tier C because compiler and flags are missing and the benchmark is a one-person repo.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust async/await versus C++20 coroutines performance evaluation paper benchmark throughput' surfaced Xavorim/cpp_tasks_bench.

name: CBQN (BQN array language) - CRLF-to-LF conversion versus plain C
language: BQN (implementation in C, SIMD kernels generated with Singeli)
baseline: Plain scalar C loop for the same line-ending conversion (crlf_to_lf), compiled with clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native
workload: Replace every CRLF with LF in a byte buffer of 100 to 1,000,000 bytes with a CRLF about every 100 characters; BQN one-liner (cr!=) with (0 shifted lf!=) filtered by Replicate versus a scalar C loop; the page also reports selection and compiler benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and reaches 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache is the bottleneck. Measured on the page (Tiger Lake i5-1135G7): C 0.555 ns/elt for 10k to 1M bytes; CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 5.2-5.9x (derived from page data); native build 0.0526 (10k), 0.0507 (30k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 7-10.6x (derived from page data). Also: selection from a small table 0.04 ns per element versus 0.2 ns, and a 35% advantage on a compiler benchmark.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: clang 15.0.7, 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' (gcc 12.2.1 also discussed: branching code, slightly faster at low density, much slower at high). CBQN built at commit 0d2631a2 with FFI, singeli x86-64 avx2 bmi2 pclmul (and a native build)
why_faster: Array primitives are implemented with hand-written SIMD, lookup tables and blocked multi-pass techniques (Replicate compresses with AVX2/AVX-512 mask operations, adapts to sparse inputs), which compilers do not generate from a scalar branching loop (no SIMD scan, movmask or compress idioms from portable C). The page itself says this is a best case: 'Your BQN programs are unlikely to outperform equivalent C programs' and specialized C is always faster.
tradeoffs: Whole-array style only: per-primitive call overhead, benefits grow with array length (hundreds to thousands of elements) and small element types; poor for sequential, data-dependent loops, cryptography with wrapping integer ops, and C++-style object dispatch. Interpreter, so C interop is through an FFI with copying. Licensing is a per-file mix with timsort (MIT) and Ryu (Apache-2.0/Boost) exceptions.
caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs and the compiler line are on the page so it is reproducible. The C baseline is a simple scalar loop the author took from a Dyalog talk, not hand-vectorized C (a SIMD C version would win; the page says so), the benchmark density of 1/100 is described as not particularly favorable, and the speedup is a best case for BQN primitives. The algorithm is not the same in the strict sense: BQN uses a data-parallel mask and Replicate, C a sequential scan. Page is dated 2023 (gcc 12.2.1, clang 15.0.7) and CBQN has changed since.
found_via: github.com/mlochbaum/BQN docs/implementation listing, page 'Performance in BQN versus C' (versusc.html); CBQN README for licensing; no WebSearch used

name: D (gdc, ldc2) matmul with std.numeric.dotProduct in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc 16.1.0 and C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, -std=c23) transposed dot-product matmul of 1500x1500 doubles
workload: Allocate, generate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices; the D version transposes b and calls std.numeric.dotProduct per output cell, the C version transposes b and runs one scalar accumulation loop.
claimed_speedup: Matmul time (median over runs, Xeon E-2324G): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, about 2.0x and 1.8x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s, Nim/gcc 3.091 s equal C. BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, Julia with OpenBLAS, Nim Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded here.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D: ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
why_faster: Derived by the searcher from the source, not stated by the suite: Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct (std/numeric.d) unrolls 16-wide with two partial sums (sum0, sum1), a different floating-point reduction order; the C loop keeps one strict-FP accumulator and is built without -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize it.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from one standard-library kernel, so a C programmer can match it by writing two or more accumulators or using -ffast-math; D's runtime and GC are not involved in the timed loop.
caveats: This is a library-kernel difference, not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm is the same (transpose plus dot products) but the D reduction order differs, so results can differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1). The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'), unlike the BLAS rows which dominate the table. CPU model and flags are stated, but gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the D compilers' LLVM/GCC bases. Time includes allocation and matrix generation.
found_via: Direct read of kostya/benchmarks README Matmul table, matmul.c, matmul.d, common/commands.mk and dlang/phobos std/numeric.d (cross-language shared suite; no WebSearch query)

name: Fortran (gfortran) matmul in plb2
baseline: C (clang 15.0.0, make flags -O3 -fwrapv -flto) 1500x1500 double matmul with the same i-k-j loop order using double** rows
workload: Multiply two 1500x1500 double-precision matrices with triple-nested loops (no BLAS), one of four plb2 tasks; Fortran version uses column-major arrays with j-k-i loops so the inner loop is unit-stride.
claimed_speedup: matmul elapsed seconds on Apple M1: Fortran gfortran 13.2.0 0.51 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, about 6% faster (derived from page data). Other compiled languages on the same row: Rust 0.56, Zig 0.56, Nim 0.56, Swift 0.56, D ldc2 0.57, V 0.57, Julia 0.76, Mojo 1.12. Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 13.2.0 with FFLAGS=-O3 (src/fortran/Makefile); C: clang 15.0.0 with CFLAGS=-O3 -fwrapv -flto (src/c/Makefile)
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (elapsed time, hyperfine)
why_faster: Not stated by the source. Searcher inference only: Fortran dummy arguments may not alias and arrays are contiguous, so gfortran can vectorize the inner loop without alias checks, whereas the C version indexes through double** rows.
tradeoffs: CC0 dedication (no patent grant). Fortran version needs gfortran; plb2 measures a naive triple loop, not tuned BLAS-level matmul.
caveats: Margin is about 6% on one machine with different compilers (gfortran versus clang) and no -flto/-march flags on the Fortran side; likely within run-to-run noise, so this is a near-tie rather than a clear win. The README says Clang already optimizes the C loop and that 'many other languages cannot'. Mechanism is the searcher's inference, which would cap a claim at C if the verifier cannot confirm it; the reproducible harness and stated compilers and CPU class are why it is kept at B. Elapsed wall time includes process startup.
found_via: Direct read of attractivechaos/plb2 README results table and src/c, src/fortran Makefiles (cross-language shared suite; no WebSearch query)

name: Halide
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C++ (OpenMP + Intel IPP), ARM NEON intrinsics/assembly and CUDA implementations of the same image-processing pipelines used as baselines in the PLDI 2013 paper (local Laplacian filters, bilateral grid, camera pipe, etc.)
workload: Image-processing pipelines written once as an algorithm plus a separate schedule (tiling, fusion, vectorization, parallelism): local Laplacian filters (99 stages) and bilateral grid on quad-core x86, plus camera raw pipe and others on ARM/CUDA, versus the hand-tuned expert code for the same pipelines.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (per search-result summary): up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA code that experts optimized over weeks or months, with 3-4x fewer lines. Results-table rows (labels matched by inference from a garbled extraction): local Laplacian 262-line C++/OpenMP+IPP vs about 62 algorithm + 7 schedule lines, 2.1x faster (secondary summary: 335 ms vs 158 ms); bilateral grid 5.9x faster, 3x shorter.
hardware: Quad-core x86 desktop, ARM and CUDA GPU platforms (exact CPU models not confirmed; paper PDF could not be opened)
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule: the programmer or autoscheduler explores loop tiling, producer-consumer fusion, recomputation vs storage, vectorization and parallelism without rewriting the algorithm, which finds locality/parallelism trade-offs that were too laborious to hand-code in C++.
tradeoffs: Embedded DSL: requires writing a Halide pipeline and a schedule (C++17 API or Python bindings), ahead-of-time or JIT compiled through LLVM; schedule quality depends on the expert or autoscheduler; image/array pipelines only, not general code. LICENSE.txt is MIT with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0.
caveats: Numbers come from the WebSearch result summary of the PLDI 2013 paper (https://people.csail.mit.edu/jrk/halide-pldi13.pdf, host not reachable from this environment, so the PDF was not opened); the summarizer itself said the table text was garbled and matched rows by inference, and the abstract's 'up to 5x' disagrees with the 5.9x table row. Baselines are the paper authors' chosen 2012-13 hand-tuned implementations (not -O3 compiled naive code) on 2012 hardware; compiler flags and CPU models not confirmed. The repository does not carry the baselines or the paper's harness, so the claim is not reproducible from the repo alone (tier B, not A). The 'language' here is a C++-embedded DSL, so Halide pipelines are callable directly from C++.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Halide vs hand-tuned C++ speedup local Laplacian bilateral grid PLDI 2013 faster lines of code' (hits: people.csail.mit.edu/jrk/halide-pldi13.pdf, commit.csail.mit.edu copy, i-programmer.info summary); repo metadata from https://github.com/halide/Halide and raw LICENSE.txt

name: Bessels.jl
baseline: SpecialFunctions.jl wrappers: openlibm (C, FreeBSD msun) j0/y0/j1/y1/jn/yn for integer-order and order-0 and 1 calls, AMOS zbes* routines (Fortran, via openspecfun) for non-integer order, so only the order-0 and order-1 rows have a C baseline
workload: Float64 evaluation of Bessel J, Y, I, K functions and gamma for random x and order nu between 0 and 100.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks (relative speed increase over SpecialFunctions.jl): besselj0 2.5x, bessely0 2.3x (the two rows whose baseline is openlibm C), besselj(nu,x) 6x, bessely(nu,x) 5x, besseli0 10x, besseli(nu,x) 7x, besselk0 10x, besselk(nu,x) 4x, Bessels.gamma 5x. README prose: 'in general 5-10x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.7.2 (no C/Fortran flags: baselines are prebuilt binary libraries)
hardware: Apple M1 run under Rosetta (x86 emulation)
why_faster: Different algorithms: piecewise polynomial/rational approximations per domain written in pure Julia that inline and vectorize, versus AMOS general-order series/recurrences and libm's older rational approximations.
tradeoffs: README admits accuracy is sometimes 'within a digit or two' of the baselines rather than better (its own error table vs ArbNumerics gives mean/max relative errors such as besselj0 3e-16/6e-14 and besselj(5.0,x) 3e-14/2e-11); positive real arguments mainly, limited complex support; Float64 focus.
caveats: First-party, run under Rosetta emulation, no compiler flags or CPU model beyond 'Apple M1', and speedups are ratios with no absolute times. Most of the baseline is Fortran AMOS, and a Fortran-vs-Julia comparison is outside this catalogue's scope; only besselj0/bessely0 (2.5x, 2.3x) are measured against C code, and the baseline goes through Julia ccall wrappers. Algorithm differs, so this is a library win, not a language win. The Bessels.gamma row is a re-export of Gamma.jl per the README, not Bessels' own code.
found_via: Direct read of JuliaMath/Bessels.jl README Benchmarks and SpecialFunctions.jl src/bessel.jl (ccall targets); no WebSearch query

name: fastGPT
baseline: PyTorch CPU inference (C++ ATen backend) of GPT-2 124M using the same BLAS (Apple Accelerate or OpenBLAS), driven by pt.py in the repo; also picoGPT (NumPy)
workload: GPT-2 124M inference, 20 generated tokens from a 19-token prompt, greedy decoding with KV cache, on Apple M1 Max at 1 to 8 cores.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks: fastGPT (Accelerate) 0.299 s vs PyTorch (Accelerate) 0.346 s (1.16x, derived); fast_tanh variant 0.288 s; OpenBLAS 1 core 0.837 s vs 0.873 s, 4 cores 0.341 s vs 0.386 s, 8 cores 0.339 s vs 0.392 s; without cache OpenBLAS 1 core 2.343 s vs PyTorch 2.356 s (parity). Total run including model load and imports: fastGPT 0.401 s vs picoGPT 3.445 s and PyTorch (OpenBLAS, 4 cores) 4.867 s.
tradeoffs: GPT-2 only, greedy sampling only, no batching or training, GGUF model conversion script needed; builds with gfortran via fpm or CMake.
caveats: First-party numbers; gfortran version and flags are not given in the README and the matmul runs through the same vendor BLAS in both programs, so the 3-13% gap is framework overhead and kernel fusion, not Fortran code generation. The README says speed comes 'by using Fortran' without a mechanism, which caps the tier at C. Baseline is PyTorch (C++ backend) rather than a C/C++ program, and the no-cache OpenBLAS rows are a tie. Only one machine and one short prompt.
found_via: Direct read of certik/fastGPT README Benchmarks section; the author's blog post 'fastGPT: faster than PyTorch in 300 lines of Fortran' is linked there (not opened)

name: llama2.mojo
baseline: karpathy/llama2.c (C, 'OMP/parallelized'; upstream 'make runomp' is gcc -Ofast -fopenmp -march=native) and llama.cpp (CPU, 6 threads)
workload: Tokens per second generating from the llama2 baby models stories15M, 42M, 110M and TinyLlama-1.1B with a parallelized, SIMD-vectorized Mojo port versus llama2.c.
claimed_speedup: README (run 2026-09-12, Mojo 1.0.0), Mac M1 Max, 8 workers: stories15M 1283 tok/s vs llama2.c 730 and llama.cpp 890; stories42M 506 vs 270 and 420; stories110M 218 vs 102 and 187 (about 1.8-2.1x llama2.c, derived). Xeon Skylake 4 vCPU AVX-512 VM: 327 vs 292, 150 vs 117, 66 vs 53, TinyLlama 6.8 vs 5.2 tok/s (1.12-1.28x derived). i7-8700: 440 vs 435, 63 vs 64 (parity). Headline: outperforms llama2.c by 30% in multi-threaded inference and llama.cpp by 20% on baby-llama.
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0; C baseline compiler and flags not stated in the README (llama2.c Makefile runomp is gcc -Ofast -fopenmp -march=native)
hardware: Apple M1 Max (8 workers); 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Skylake AVX-512 VM, Ubuntu 26.04; Intel Core i7-8700 3.2 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04
why_faster: README: leverages Mojo's SIMD and vectorization primitives plus a persistent worker pool for parallelize; llama2.c relies on compiler auto-vectorization and OpenMP.
tradeoffs: Needs the Mojo toolchain (Mojo compiler and MAX packages from Modular; the compiler is not an OSI-licensed open-source project), only llama2 stories models and TinyLlama; the repo license (MIT) applies to the port itself.
caveats: First-party table; compile flags and compiler for the C baseline, thread counts of llama.cpp and run counts are not given, and the margin disappears on the i7-8700 (parity, 63 vs 64 tok/s on stories110M). llama2.c is a deliberately simple baseline. An independent run on M1 Max is linked ('mojo vs 6 programming languages' on engiware.com) but could not be opened. Mojo numbers depend on the tuned matmul tiling in this port rather than on the language alone.
found_via: Direct read of tairov/llama2.mojo README (llama2.c port family, cross-language numerics); karpathy/llama2.c Makefile for the baseline flags; no WebSearch query

name: llama2.zig (cgbur)
baseline: karpathy/llama2.c built with 'make runfast -march=native' (gcc -Ofast), single-threaded; also plain 'make run -march=native' (-O3)
workload: stories15M.bin inference, 256 tokens, single-threaded, argmax and top-p 0.9 sampling, on AMD Ryzen 9 5900X.
claimed_speedup: README, single-threaded argmax (temperature 0): llama2.zig 660 tok/s vs llama2.c runfast 548 (1.20x, derived) vs llama2.c run (-O3) 122; top-p: 579 vs 463 (1.25x, derived). Multi-threaded: llama2.c runomp 1564 tok/s, llama2.zig has no multithreading and is not compared.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.11.0-dev.4315+f5239677e; C baseline 'make runfast -march=native' (upstream Makefile: gcc -Ofast) with the C compiler version not stated
why_faster: README: SIMD matrix multiplication with Zig @Vector (about 115 to 430 tok/s from that change alone), comptime-generated fused matmul, vector-aligned allocation and SIMD versions of other core functions.

Last commit only pinned CI, so the benchmark was not rerun.
found_via: Direct read of cgbur/llama2.zig README Performance section (llama2.c port family, cross-language numerics); no WebSearch query

name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (SciML)
baseline: Sundials ARKODE and CVODE (C), with Hairer dopri5/dop853 and LSODA (Fortran) via ODEInterface as secondary baselines, compared at matched tolerances in work-precision diagrams
workload: Work-precision (runtime versus error) comparison of ODE solvers on non-stiff and stiff test problems (rigid body, linear systems, Lotka-Volterra, Filament PDE and others) in SciMLBenchmarks.jl.
claimed_speedup: SciMLBenchmarks README summary, no numbers on the page: non-stiff 'OrdinaryDiffEq.jl's methods are the most efficient by a good amount', the Vern methods do best in every non-stiff benchmark, ARKODE and Hairer dopri5/dop853 are far less efficient than the Vern methods, CVODE_Adams and lsoda do not do well; stiff: ARKODE is inconsistent and OrdinaryDiffEq KenCarp4 is much more efficient in most cases.
why_faster: Different integrators: high-order Verner and Tsitouras pairs with cheap interpolants and type-specialized, inlined right-hand sides compiled in Julia, compared with Dormand-Prince or multistep methods in the C/Fortran libraries.
tradeoffs: Julia package ecosystem and JIT warmup latency; wins depend on the problem and the chosen method, and the README says stiff results are 'much more problem dependent'.
caveats: The numbers live in work-precision plots on docs.sciml.ai (not reachable from this environment), so no figure could be quoted and the README text is the only evidence; first-party benchmark repository with public jmd sources but no hardware or compiler line seen here. The Rigid Body page notes some of the gap depends on the error norm used by each library. Comparison is algorithm versus algorithm (Vern9 versus dopri5/ARKODE), not same-method language comparison; Fortran baselines are out of scope and Sundials (C) is the in-scope baseline.
found_via: WebSearch: 'OrdinaryDiffEq.jl faster than Fortran dop853 and Sundials C++ benchmark speedup Julia differential equations solvers outperform' (returned only qualitative docs.sciml.ai pages); README read from raw.githubusercontent.com/SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl, RigidBody_wpd.jmd for the solver list
